content: Your doctor has prescribed cefazolin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication can be administered either by injection into a large muscle, such as the buttock or hip, or through an intravenous (IV) infusion. If given intravenously, the drug will be added to a fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over a 30-minute period, typically two to four times daily. Cefazolin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including those affecting the lungs, skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, heart valves, and urinary tract. In some cases, cefazolin may be prescribed for other conditions; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting cefazolin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to cefazolin, other cephalosporins, penicillins, or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs you are taking, including other antibiotics, probenecid (Benemid), and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal diseases, particularly colitis. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while taking cefazolin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and routinely check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape for testing, as cefazolin may cause false-positive results with Clinitest tablets. Before administering cefazolin, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it or observing it closely. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop the treatment on your own, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. Cefazolin may cause side effects. If the medication is injected into a muscle, it may be combined with lidocaine (Xylocaine) to reduce pain at the injection site. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they are severe or persistent: diarrhea, stomach pain, upset stomach, or vomiting. However, if you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your healthcare provider immediately: skin rash, itching, hives, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, or a sore mouth or throat. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving cefazolin intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days' worth of medication at a time. Store the medication in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional doses in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving cefazolin intramuscularly, follow your healthcare provider's storage instructions carefully. Keep all supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving cefazolin intravenously or subcutaneously, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection, which can occur at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. Cefazolin is also marketed under the brand name Ancef®.
